33 An electric kettle is marked 3.10 kW. It is used with an electrical supply of 240 V.
What is the electric current in the kettle and what is the kettle’s electrical resistance when
working?
current / A
resistance / Ω
A
0.0129
18 600
B
0.0770
3100
C
12.9
18.6
D
12.9
3100

hints: Start from the two numbers printed on the kettle: power $3.10 \text{ kW} = 3100 \text{ W}$ and supply voltage $240 \text{ V}$.
Recall that electrical power links those two quantities by $P = VI$, so current is $I = P/V$ with units $\text{A}$.
Then use $V = IR$ for the heating element, so $R = V/I$ or $R = V^2/P$, and check the result is in $\Omega$ near $20 \text{ }\Omega$, not thousands of ohms.
walkthrough: Convert the rated power to watts: $P = 3.10 \text{ kW} = 3100 \text{ W}$, with $V = 240 \text{ V}$ across the kettle when working.
Use power in terms of current and voltage: $P = VI$. Rearrange for current: $I = P/V$.
Substitute values with units: $I = 3100/240 \text{ A} \approx 12.9 \text{ A}$.
Use resistance from Ohm's law $V = IR$, so $R = V/I$. Substitute: $R = 240/12.9 \text{ }\Omega \approx 18.6 \text{ }\Omega$.
Equivalently $R = V^2/P = 240^2/3100 \text{ }\Omega \approx 18.6 \text{ }\Omega$, confirming the unit check $\text{V A}^{-1} = \Omega$.
The pair $12.9 \text{ A}$ and $18.6 \text{ }\Omega$ matches the table row. This is option C

A.explanation: Divides voltage by power incorrectly and gives a milliamp-scale current and kilo-ohm resistance, far too small a current for a $3100 \text{ W}$ heater at $240 \text{ V}$.

B.explanation: Gives a current about 100 times too small, as if power in $\text{W}$ was confused with power in $\text{kW}$ without converting $3.10 \text{ kW}$ to $3100 \text{ W}$.

C.explanation: Current $I = P/V \approx 12.9 \text{ A}$ and resistance $R = V/I \approx 18.6 \text{ }\Omega$ satisfy both $P = VI$ and $V = IR$.

D.explanation: Current $12.9 \text{ A}$ is correct but $3100 \text{ }\Omega$ does not satisfy $R = V/I$; it repeats the power number as resistance.
